title: He Took His Own Show Off the Internet to Survive. Now Samay Raina's 'India's Got Latent' Is a Netflix Original.
excerpt: Sixteen months after pulling every episode private under fire, the comedian returns with a Netflix–YouTube simulcast, 15 million views in hours, and Alia Bhatt in the guest chair.
body:
Sixteen months ago, **Samay Raina** pulled his own show off the internet in the dead of night. Every episode of *India's Got Latent* went private on a single February evening in 2025, the comedian's gamble at containing a wildfire that had already jumped the firebreak — police complaints, the National Commission for Women, an editor briefly arrested, effigies burning over remarks a guest had made on his panel. He later said it "broke me." It looked, for a while, like the end of the most chaotic, most watched experiment Indian internet comedy had ever produced.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=fZWbECgYVIY</youtube>

Now look at him. *India's Got Latent* Season 2 premiered on June 20 — not on a scrappy YouTube channel this time, but on **Netflix**, simulcast to 190-odd countries, with the streamer's own marketing muscle behind it. The premiere reportedly crossed **fifteen million views within hours**. The man who took his show down to survive has come back with the biggest distribution deal a creator-led property in India has ever landed. If that isn't the most satisfying redemption arc of the year, name a better one.

> "His show's first season couldn't have ended on a higher note." — Samay Raina, in his April stand-up special *Still Alive*

That line was pure Samay — deadpan, a little defiant, refusing to let the controversy write his ending for him. The bodyguard from *Still Alive*, **Amin Khan**, became the unlikely face of the comeback teaser Netflix dropped on June 19, a wink to fans who'd followed every twist. The format hasn't changed: contestants perform some gloriously unhinged "latent" talent, then predict the exact score the panel will hand them, win cash if they nail it, and absorb the roast either way. What's changed is the stage. Bigger budget, glossier production, and a panel that now pulls A-listers.

And what an opening move. The first episode handed its guest-judge chairs to **Alia Bhatt** and **Sharvari**, who showed up mid-promotional-blitz for their YRF spy film *Alpha*. It was a canny piece of cross-pollination — two of Bollywood's most-watched women parked on the internet's most unpredictable couch, lending the show their wattage while borrowing its reach. Watching Alia, all polished movie-star ease, try to keep a straight face through whatever bizarre act walked on is exactly the collision *Latent* was built for. The high and the low, the multiplex and the meme, sharing one frame.

The Netflix–YouTube dual drop is the real strategic stroke, and Samay can't resist needling the difference. Netflix viewers get an ad-free, polished cut; YouTube viewers, he joked, lose the right to leave comments — the lifeblood of the original's chaotic energy. New episodes land every two weeks on both platforms, a cadence designed to keep the discourse perpetually simmering rather than burning out in a weekend binge. **Balraj Singh Ghai** returns alongside Samay as a fixed judge, with a rotating bench of comedians and creators — **Aashish Solanki** among the early guests — keeping the panel chemistry loose.

For the diaspora, this is the headline buried in the format notes: *Latent* is now a **Netflix Original**, which means an NRI in New Jersey or a student in Manchester can stream it the same hour it drops, no VPN gymnastics, no hunting for reuploads. The show that once felt like an in-joke you had to be terminally online and India-based to follow is now a tap away on the same app serving up *Squid Game*. That's a genuine shift. Indian internet humour — its specific cadence, its Hindi-English code-switching, its references that don't translate in subtitles — is being handed a global shelf without being sanded down for it.

There's a real question humming under the celebration, of course. The thing that made Season 1 magnetic was its uncensored, anything-goes nerve — and that same nerve is what nearly ended it. A Netflix banner brings standards, lawyers, and a compliance team that a YouTube channel never had. Can *Latent* keep its edge wrapped in corporate cellophane, or does the streamer's polish dull the very blade that made it dangerous? The early numbers say audiences don't care about the philosophy — they just want the show back.

Samay Raina spent 2025 watching his creation get pulled apart in headlines. He spent 2026 turning it into a Netflix tentpole. Whatever you think of the show, that's a comeback with some swagger. New episode in a fortnight. The latent talents of India are not done with us yet.
